query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a post-process heat treatment to AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock used in additive manufacturing can overcome residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock in as-additively-manufactured condition
generation.conditions: Heat treatment temperatures ranging from 500 °C to 1100 °C, with a holding time of 6 hours
generation.mechanism: Relief of residual thermal stresses, regulation of phase proportions and phase boundary structures, and enhancement of mechanical properties through grain refinement and precipitation evolution
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical properties, such as strength and ductility, and reduced processing complexity
generation.baseline: Components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions without heat treatment
generation.boundary: Heat treatment temperatures above 1100 °C may lead to significant changes in phase structure and degradation of mechanical properties
generation.uncertainty: Optimal heat treatment parameters, such as temperature and holding time, may vary depending on the specific alloy composition and additive manufacturing process

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi components with and without post-process heat treatment
measurements: Microstructural characterization (phase structure, grain size, eutectic morphology)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated components do not exhibit improved mechanical properties and reduced processing complexity compared to the non-heat-treated components, the hypothesis is falsified

Laser additive manufacturing (LAM) offers unparalleled advantages in the efficient and high-precision fabrication of components with complex geometries, surpassing traditional manufacturing methods []. The exceptional casting ability of EHEAs enables their effective integration with AM techniques, facilitating the production of high-quality, high-performance structural parts [,]. However, the AM process involves rapid solidification, resulting in non-equilibrium atomic arrangements and interfacial configurations. The wide variety of additive manufacturing technologies and types of EHEAs leads to significant differences in both the microstructure and macrostructure of fabricated alloy components. Furthermore, the selection of heat treatment processes critically influences these structural characteristics at both microscopic and macroscopic scales. Consequently, establishing clear application-driven relationships among additive manufacturing technologies, alloy types, and heat treatment parameters presents a complex challenge in this field. Addressing this challenge will significantly advance the engineering application and widespread adoption of EHEA-based additive components. However, resolving this issue requires concerted efforts from researchers to systematically develop and refine comprehensive models that correlate additive manufacturing methods, alloy compositions, and heat treatment protocols.

High-purity argon gas (99.999%) was used as a protective atmosphere during melting. To ensure compositional homogeneity, the melting process was repeated four times. ## 2.3. Mechanical Properties
Wire cutting was used to prepare cylindrical samples with a diameter of 4 mm and a height of 6 mm for compression testing. Compression tests were conducted using a CSS-44100 electronic universal testing machine (CCTM, Changchun, China) at a constant loading rate of 1 mm/min. For each material condition, two compression test specimens were prepared, and the final mechanical data were derived through fitting procedures. The compression test followed the ASTM E9 standard []. The fracture surfaces of the tested samples were examined using the SEM to analyze the failure mechanisms and gain insights into the material’s behavior under mechanical stress.
